opus-5.5.text:
Look, I want to be upfront: I don't think every state law is a good law. Some of the proposals out there are poorly thought through. A blanket ban on training a model to offer any emotional support is a good example. It's well-intentioned, because people are worried about vulnerable users, but it's written so broadly that it could sweep in things that genuinely help people. So I share the concern that a patchwork of fifty different state regimes, some of them not very well designed, is a real problem.

But a ten-year moratorium is the wrong answer to that problem. It's far too blunt an instrument. Ten years is an enormous amount of time in this field. Think about where AI was ten years ago compared to now. And I think the next few years will bring far more change than the last ten. We could plausibly have systems that match or exceed human capability across a wide range of tasks within that window. Saying, in effect, "nobody at the state level can act, and we have no federal framework to replace it," means locking in a vacuum during what may be the most consequential period for this technology.

That's the core of it: preemption without a federal standard isn't a policy, it's an absence of policy. If the federal government said, "Here is a national framework, and we want it to be uniform, so states shouldn't layer their own rules on top," I'd be much more open to that. Preemption is a reasonable tool when it comes with something real. What I've advocated for is a federal transparency standard. Frontier developers should have to publicly disclose how they test their models for serious risks, such as national security risks, biological and cyber misuse, and autonomy risks, and what they do to mitigate them. Many of the leading companies, including us, already do a version of this voluntarily. But as models get more powerful and commercial pressure gets more intense, I don't think we should rely on voluntary commitments holding forever. Making it law creates a floor.

So my position isn't "states good, federal bad," or the reverse. It's that we need some guardrails, they should be light-touch and focused on the most serious risks rather than micromanaging every use case, and ideally they'd be set at the federal level. Until that exists, tying everyone's hands for a decade is a bet I'm not willing to make. The bad state laws are a reason to write a good federal law, not a reason to have no law at all.

r001.rationale: It says preemption without a federal standard leaves a policy vacuum, with no federal framework to replace state rules.

r002.rationale: It calls ten years an enormous amount of time and links the period to rapidly advancing AI and potentially human-level capabilities.

r003.rationale: It says federal preemption would be reasonable if paired with a national framework that provides a substantive standard.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I want to be clear up front: I'm not a fan of a lot of these state bills. Something like the Tennessee proposal, banning training a model to provide emotional support, that's a good example of a law that's responding to a real concern but in a way that's clumsy and probably counterproductive. People use these systems to talk through hard things in their lives, and the right answer is standards around how that's done safely, not a flat prohibition. So if the argument for the moratorium is "some of these state laws are bad," I actually agree with the premise. I just think the conclusion is wrong.

Here's why. A ten-year moratorium is an extraordinarily blunt instrument applied to the fastest-moving technology in history. Ten years ago we had models that could barely write a coherent paragraph. Ten years from now, if the trends hold, we may have systems that are smarter than most humans at most cognitive tasks, running companies, doing science. Nobody can tell you what the right regulatory framework for that world looks like. So the idea of saying, in advance, that for the next decade one entire layer of our government is forbidden from acting, with nothing put in its place, that's not a policy. That's an absence of policy dressed up as one.

And that's the crux of it: the moratorium preempts states without replacing them with anything. If Congress passed a real federal framework, transparency requirements, safety testing for frontier models, disclosure of how models behave, I'd be the first to say that should supersede a patchwork of fifty different state regimes. We've said that publicly. A patchwork is genuinely bad for companies like us and for smaller companies even more. But that's not what's on the table. What's on the table is "states, stop, and the federal government will get around to it." I've been in Washington enough to know what "get around to it" means.

The other thing I'd say is that the fear of patchwork is somewhat overstated relative to the fear of doing nothing. Most of the serious state proposals are actually fairly convergent, they're about transparency, about not lying to the public about your safety practices. That's a low bar, and frankly it's a bar the responsible labs already clear. The problem cases, like the emotional support ban, tend to get fixed or die on their own because they're unpopular and unworkable. The democratic process at the state level is messy, but it's a process. The moratorium short-circuits it.

So my position is: fix the bad laws, pass a good federal standard, and let that federal standard preempt. Don't use the existence of a few bad state bills as the excuse to take the entire country's regulatory capacity offline for a decade during exactly the window when we're going to find out whether this technology is as powerful as I think it is.

r001.rationale: It says the moratorium preempts states “without replacing them with anything” and contrasts that with a federal framework.

r002.rationale: It calls ten years excessive for fast-moving AI and describes major capability changes, but does not clearly relate that duration to timelines for serious AI risks.

r003.rationale: It conditionally supports federal preemption if Congress establishes a real federal framework with substantive requirements such as transparency and safety testing.

astra-6.text:
I think you can oppose a particular state law and also think that a ten-year moratorium is a bad idea. Those aren’t contradictory positions. A restriction on training AI to provide emotional support could rule out things that are helpful to people. We should evaluate that law on its merits.

But ten years is an extraordinarily long time for this technology. We don’t know what these systems will be capable of in two or three years, let alone ten. If you prevent states from acting without putting a substantive federal framework in place, you’re potentially leaving a very large gap.

I’d prefer a sensible national framework. There are real costs to having fifty different sets of requirements. But the argument for federal preemption should be that the federal government is addressing the problem effectively. The existence of some bad state proposals isn’t enough to justify taking away the ability of every state to respond to risks we may discover.

r001.rationale: It warns that a moratorium without a substantive federal framework could leave a large gap and remove states’ ability to respond to risks.

r002.rationale: It calls ten years extraordinarily long, noting major capability changes could happen within two or three years and risks may be discovered during that period.

r003.rationale: It favors a national framework and says federal preemption is justified when the federal government is effectively addressing the problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you can oppose a particular state law without concluding that states should be prohibited from doing anything about AI for ten years. Those are very different positions.

A ban on training models to provide emotional support sounds overly broad to me. There are beneficial uses there, and we should distinguish those from situations where a model encourages someone’s delusions or gives dangerous advice. Regulate the actual harm, and be careful about cutting off the benefits.

But ten years is an extraordinarily long time in this technology. If the federal government says, “We’re going to establish sensible national standards, and those will preempt conflicting state rules,” that’s a conversation worth having. If it says, “States can’t act,” without putting an adequate federal framework in place, you’ve potentially created a vacuum during a period of enormous change.

I’d much prefer a coherent federal approach. But the existence of bad state proposals isn’t sufficient reason to eliminate every state’s ability to respond to problems we may not even anticipate today.

r001.rationale: It opposes barring states from acting when no adequate federal framework is in place, warning that this could create a regulatory vacuum.

r002.rationale: It calls ten years extraordinarily long for the technology, but does not connect that duration to the timeline of serious AI risks.

r003.rationale: It says federal standards that preempt conflicting state rules are worth considering, conditional on establishing sensible national standards.
